title: Container, Cargo, and Chargeable: How Weight Rules Every Freight Quote
meta_title: Tare, Net, and Gross Weight in Shipping Explained
meta_description: Tare, net, and gross weight explained: VGM filings, the DIM formula, and how container weight drives freight costs.
body_markdown:
Take 1,000 boxes at 10 kg each. The goods alone weigh 10,000 kg. Add a 40-ft container with a tare of 3,800 kg and your gross weight lands at 13,800 kg. That single arithmetic chain, net plus tare equals gross, sits underneath customs clearance, VGM filings, axle limits, and every freight quote you will ever receive. Get one number wrong and the whole stack shifts.

## Where the numbers come from
Net weight is the goods by themselves: no container, no crate, no covering. Tare weight is the opposite extreme, an empty trailer, truck, or container with nothing inside. Gross weight combines them, folding in everything wrapped around the goods: pallets, packaging, dunnage.
A container's tare is usually printed right on its exterior, but the figure depends on which box you book. Expect roughly 2,200 kg, about 4,850 lbs, from a 20-ft dry unit. The 40-ft dry version sits near 3,800 kg (8,380 lbs). Choose the high cube and the empty box already weighs around 4,200 kg, or 9,260 lbs, before a single carton goes in.
Those figures feed directly into Verified Gross Mass submissions and into how you distribute cargo inside the unit. A wrong tare figure corrupts everything downstream of it, and compliance problems tend to be expensive ones.

## What a bad declaration actually costs
Carriers, customs officers, and compliance authorities all price and plan around the weight you declare. When that declaration is wrong or thin on detail, the consequences run from annoying to severe: overloaded containers raising compliance concerns, route restrictions that knock delivery schedules off track, unexpected upcharges inflating freight fees, and SOLAS violations, most often traced to skipped or sloppy VGM submissions.
At sea, the SOLAS regime requires shippers to submit verified tare, net, and gross weights before the vessel sails. Miss that step and you can face port pushback, suspended shipping, or penalties. Standard boxes come with ceilings you have to respect. The 20-ft carries about 2.2 tonnes of tare against a max gross near 24 tonnes. Its 40-ft sibling begins around 3.8 tonnes of tare and tops out close to 30 tonnes gross.
On European roads, exceeding gross vehicle weight (GVW) invites fines and roadside checks, and correct container loading keeps axle balance in check. Air freight plays by yet another rulebook, built around dimensional weight rather than GVW or VGM.

## The air freight formula worth memorizing
Air carriers charge on chargeable weight. They compare the shipment's actual weight against its cubic DIM weight and bill whichever figure is greater, so the larger of the two becomes the cost-driving figure:
(L x W x H in cm) ÷ 6,000 = DIM weight in kg
Light, bulky cargo gets punished here. The 6,000 divisor means volume, not heft, can decide what you pay.

## How weight shows up on the invoice
Freight pricing bends around weight in different ways depending on the mode:
- With LCL, the price keys off how heavy or how bulky your cargo is, so fees shift with scale or space.
- FCL comes with firm weight ceilings; cross them and surcharges appear while schedules slow down.
- A stated weight that turns out wrong can push you into a bigger container, or into flat racks when the shipment is oversized.
Overweight cargo goes further than surcharges. Carriers can cancel bookings outright, and surprise freight fees follow close behind. Exceeding gross weight guidelines also risks terminal rejections and genuine safety hazards in transit.

## Taking manual math out of the loop
Most weight errors start as human error. Load planning software attacks that directly. It keeps weight entries from being mistyped, matches the container to what the cargo actually measures, confirms VGM and SOLAS compliance, flags rules tied to the route, and catches containers that were loaded wrong or paired badly.
The SeaRates Load Calculator puts this to work for shippers. It works out tare, net, and gross figures for the container, breaks weights down by category, generates space-efficient 3D load plans that keep the cargo balanced, and runs through shipment scenarios in advance so stacking or spacing problems surface before anything ships.
Weight touches every shipment three times over: as a legal question, as a logistics question, and as a question of liability. Accuracy is protection. Penalties, postponed deliveries, and disputes over price all stay outside the door when your numbers hold up.
